analysis.one_liner: Banned pulp and paper mills from discharging chlorine compounds into waterways after five years.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote; despite 56 cosponsors, it sat in a House subcommittee until the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: The Chlorine Zero Discharge Act would have amended the Clean Water Act to require every pulp and paper mill that uses chlorine in its process to stop releasing organochlorine compounds into water — absolutely zero output, not just trace amounts — five years after enactment. It would have required federal permits to enforce that standard, directed the EPA to study chlorine-free bleaching technology and help mills switch to it, and created an advisory panel with public hearings to recommend next categories of organochlorine discharges to phase out. The bill was introduced in August 1993, referred to the Public Works and Transportation Committee, sent to its Water Resources and Environment Subcommittee, and never came up again.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near or downstream of pulp and paper mills — the communities whose rivers, lakes, and fisheries receive the discharges, including the Great Lakes region the bill's findings invoke. Organochlorines from chlorine bleaching include dioxins, which persist in the environment and build up in the food chain, reaching humans who eat contaminated fish. The bill would also have given the public, for the first time, a national accounting of which facilities discharge how much organochlorine into water.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every pulp and paper facility using chlorine to achieve zero discharge of organochlorine compounds into water within five years of enactment, with permits rewritten to enforce it.
Defines zero discharge as absolutely no release, including nonpoint runoff — not merely a less-than-detectable level — closing the usual regulatory loophole that allows trace ongoing pollution.

Directs the EPA to evaluate chlorine-free bleaching alternatives, publish a report on the technology transition, and provide technical support to mills switching, rather than imposing costs without a path to compliance.

Requires an EPA report listing every category of industrial and nonpoint organochlorine discharge into water, quantities by facility, and facility locations — a public record of who is polluting what.

Creates a 15-member advisory panel including public health, occupational health, and ecology experts plus affected citizens, labor, and industry, required to hold public hearings — a defined public voice in the next phase-out recommendations.

analysis.who_pays: Pulp and paper mill owners bear the cost of converting from chlorine bleaching to chlorine-free technology within five years. Chlorine and chlorinated-chemical suppliers lose the pulp and paper market. Some of the cost would pass through to buyers of bleached paper products, and workers at mills that could not convert in time would bear the risk to their jobs.

drawbacks.text: The zero-discharge definition is absolute — 'absolutely no output or release' and explicitly 'not a less than detectable output or release' — leaving mills no tolerance for trace residues even if treatment removes nearly all of it, a standard stricter than any then in force.

A five-year deadline to retool every chlorine-bleached mill carried real risk of plant closures in one-industry mill towns and higher paper prices in the interim, a cost the bill acknowledged only by having EPA assist with the transition rather than by phasing the deadline.

The bill targeted only pulp and paper discharges; its own text shows the broader organochlorine phase-out it envisions depended on future reports and recommendations that could have taken years more to translate into rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health case was substantial: the bill's findings recite that persistent bioaccumulative toxins like the organochlorines from chlorine bleaching are biologically active at infinitesimal doses and concentrate up the food chain to humans, and the Great Lakes commission had already endorsed zero discharge as the goal. The conversion costs were real but not speculative forever — chlorine-free bleaching technology existed and the bill funded EPA assistance for the switch. The main design weakness is the absolute standard and tight five-year clock, which gave struggling mills little flexibility; a longer phase-in with a trace-tolerance floor would have softened the transition risk at some cost to the environmental goal.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in August 1993, the bill was referred to the House Public Works and Transportation Committee, which sent it to its Water Resources and Environment Subcommittee, where it stayed until the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995 without a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Bill Richardson (D-NM) introduced the Chlorine Zero Discharge Act of 1993 on August 5, 1993, joined by 12 original cosponsors including Henry Waxman, and it was referred to the House Committee on Public Works and Transportation.
On August 19, 1993, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment, which was its last recorded action.

The bill accumulated 56 cosponsors — 54 Democrats, one Independent, and one Republican — but the committee and subcommittee never acted on it, and no version ever reached the House floor or the Senate before the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pulp and paper mills that bleach with chlorine, and the chemical suppliers that serve them, came out ahead: they faced no zero-discharge mandate, no permit rewrite, and no conversion deadline, and communities near the mills continued to absorb the discharges.

for.name: Bill Richardson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it broad if overwhelmingly Democratic support.

against.name: House Committee on Public Works and Transportation
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by a Democrat in the 103rd Congress
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote; the subcommittee referral on August 19, 1993 was the last entry in its history.

against.name: Pulp and paper industry
against.role: Operators of chlorine-bleached pulp and paper mills
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandatory zero-discharge deadlines for chlorine bleaching, favoring less absolute effluent standards; the record of this bill contains no markup or vote in which that opposition appears formally.

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Democratic — 54 of 56 cosponsors, with one Republican and one Independent — but the bill never got a vote in either chamber, so the full chambers' positions were never measured.

industries.industry: Pulp and paper mills that bleach with chlorine
industries.note: The bill would have required these mills to eliminate organochlorine discharges within five years and rewrite their permits accordingly, forcing conversion to chlorine-free bleaching technology. Their avoided compliance cost is the discharge burden that mill-adjacent communities keep bearing.

Pulp and paper is a major industrial market for chlorine; a mandated switch to chlorine-free bleaching would have stripped much of that demand. The industry's interest in keeping the chlorine market intact runs against cleaner water downstream.

industries.industry: Producers of chlorine-free bleaching equipment and technology
industries.note: The bill would have driven a wholesale technology transition to chlorine-free pulping, with EPA technical support helping mills buy and implement the alternatives — a windfall for the suppliers of that equipment.
